items.title: CodeQL changes for macOS 27, Xcode 27, and Swift 6.4
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Starting with macOS 27 and Xcode 27, Apple no longer includes Intel (x86_64) code in some of the system binaries and libraries that CodeQL relies on to trace builds. As a result, CodeQL can’t support traced scans on these versions or analyze Swift 6.4. What’s affected Xcode 27: When Xcode 27 is installed, traced extraction isn’t available for C/C++, C#, Go, Java, Kotlin, or Swift. macOS 27: Traced extraction may not be available for the previously mentioned languages. Swift 6.4: CodeQL doesn’t support Swift 6.4 on any platform. Intel-based Macs: CodeQL support for Intel-based Macs will be deprecated in mid-December 2026. How to keep your scans running If you scan Swift or use traced builds for other languages, pin your workflows to macOS 26 or earlier and Xcode 26 or earlier. If you use GitHub Actions, pin the runner image and toolchain in your workflow rather than relying on the latest versions. For C/C++, C#, and Java, you can switch to build mode none, which doesn’t require tracing a build. Join the discussion within GitHub Community. The post CodeQL changes for macOS 27, Xcode 27, and Swift 6.4 appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: CodeQL is dropping traced scans on macOS 27/Xcode 27 and support for Swift 6.4. This mainly affects iOS and native projects, not our core web stack.

items.title: Copilot model policy API for enterprise, orgs, and teams
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: You can now use the REST API to retrieve and update Copilot model policies for enterprises, enterprise teams, enterprise apps, and organizations. What’s new GET and PATCH endpoints are now generally available for model policies at four levels: Enterprise: /enterprises/{enterprise}/copilot/model-policies Enterprise teams: /enterprises/{enterprise}/teams/{team_slug}/copilot/model-policies Enterprise apps: /enterprises/{enterprise}/copilot/apps/model-policies Organization: /orgs/{org}/copilot/model-policies Together, these endpoints make it easier to manage Copilot model availability across your enterprise. Enterprise policies can delegate model control to organizations in organization mode, or to teams and apps in enterprise teams mode. Reference our documentation on managing availability of models in your enterprise and our REST API documentation to get started. The post Copilot model policy API for enterprise, orgs, and teams appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: Copilot model policies are now manageable through the REST API at enterprise and org levels. Useful when advising clients who standardize on Copilot governance.

items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: As of today, October 19, 2026, we have deprecated the following models across most GitHub Copilot experiences (including Copilot Chat, inline edits, ask and agent modes, and code completions). These deprecations were announced on September 18, 2026. Model Deprecation date Suggested alternative Gemini 3.7 Flash 2026-10-19 Gemini 3.8 Flash GPT-5.5 2026-10-19 GPT-6.1 Sol GPT-5.4 2026-10-19 GPT-6.1 Sol GPT-5.4 mini 2026-10-19 GPT-6 Luna GPT-5 mini 2026-10-19 GPT-6 Luna Grok 4.5 2026-10-19 Grok 4.7 Please update your workflows and integrations to use supported models. items.why_it_matters: Copilot deprecated GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.7 Flash and others as of today. Client teams on Copilot must move workflows and integrations to the newer replacement models.

items.title: Some Git over HTTPS may temporarily require authentication
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: During periods of unusual traffic, GitHub may temporarily require authentication for some clones and fetches of public repositories over HTTPS to help protect github.com’s availability. If an operation is affected, it will fail with a message indicating that authentication is required. To continue, authenticate and retry the operation. You can also wait and retry without authentication after the temporary protection has been lifted. GitHub applies this protection as narrowly as possible using signals associated with anomalous traffic. Because legitimate and anomalous traffic can sometimes share those signals, legitimate unauthenticated operations may occasionally be affected. This is not a general authentication requirement for public repositories. The following operations are unaffected: Authenticated Git operations over HTTPS Git operations over SSH Pushes Unrelated GitHub web and API traffic For more reliable automated clones and fetches, configure authentication: GitHub Actions: Use the built-in GITHUB_TOKEN. Other CI systems: Prefer a GitHub App installation access token. A personal access token can also be used. Operations that cannot authenticate: Retry after the temporary protection has been lifted. This protection applies to repositories on github.com across all plans. For setup instructions, see about authentication to GitHub and managing remote repositories. The post Some Git over HTTPS may temporarily require authentication appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
items.why_it_matters: GitHub may require authentication for public repo clones over HTTPS during anomalous traffic. Unauthenticated CI jobs, GitHub Actions steps and agent sandboxes could fail unexpectedly.

items.excerpt: What's changed Added a transcript line when a plugin that runs first skips one of your mod's hooks, naming the event and the plugin Added decider: "person" to a mod's tool.check answer: only the permission dialog or a host's callback can approve the ask, and it is refused with the mod's reason where nobody can be asked Added e.isReadOnly to a mod's tool.check event, set when the tool call is read-only Added /auto-mode-setup: a guided setup that reads your project and recent sessions to teach auto mode about your environment, now also available on Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, Claude apps gateway and telemetry-disabled sessions Added /claude-api managed-agents-secure, which compares a Managed Agents agent's settings with Anthropic's published security guide, without changing anything Added the names of the tools called earlier to the compaction summary in the transcript view (Ctrl+O) Added a warning on Pro and Max plans when resuming an inactive conversation would use a noticeable share of your 5-hour usage limit: resume anyway, or start a new conversation and Claude can look up the previous one if you refer to it Fixed the organization policy not refreshing until the hourly check after approving an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY at startup or switching "Use custom API key" in /config Fixed sandboxed commands failing to start on Linux when a sandbox.filesystem.denyRead glob contains brackets that are not a character class, such as a [user-id] route folder Fixed rm -r of a mounted drive or a folder at its top level (/Volumes, /media, WSL's /mnt/c) not getting the safety prompt that rm -rf /Applications gets Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_TRANSCRIPT_LOCAL_GC dropping messages from the saved transcript when the disk filled up while the file was being trimmed Fixed a plugin keeping a headless run going past --max-turns, Stop, or ended input by spawning subagents or re-running a finished one Fixed a failed mod reload removing the tools and commands of the version that stays loaded, and its messages be
items.why_it_matters: Claude Code release with substantive changes: new hook and permission controls for mods, read-only detection on tool checks, and a guided /auto-mode-setup. These directly affect our gated agent workflows.

items.title: Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?
items.author: rzk
items.excerpt: I saw this LinkedIn post from a Meta engineer and it resonated with me:https://www.linkedin.com/posts/ali-hamie_im-an-engineer-at-m...> I'm an engineer at Meta and I never felt this uncomfortable doing my job. I'm writing code these days and it all feels like a black box. This new standard of shipping with AI is moving so fast that if we're going to spend our time checking each line of code, it's going to take forever. That means you can end up with systems you've built where you don't truly understand how all the code works. You understand the high level, but not every detail. And maybe this is becoming the new standard. It goes against every instinct of being a software engineer. I'm used to understanding what I'm building. Now I'm trying to figure out how much I need to understand before I'm comfortable moving forward. Are other engineers feeling this too?How are you handling this? Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50151036 Points: 187 # Comments: 306
items.why_it_matters: Discussion on shipping AI-written code you don't fully understand. This speaks directly to our verification-over-vibes practice and to how we review agent output.

items.title: llm-echo 0.5
items.excerpt: Release: llm-echo 0.5 I'm working towards a new LLM release, and testing PRs caused me to revisit the llm-echo debug plugin. This plugin provides a "model" which doesn't involve an LLM at all - it just repeats back the prompts that have been fed to it. The new release now updates the simulated token usage counts to take tool calls, system prompts, and reasoning tokens into account. Example usage: uvx --with llm-echo llm -m echo 'hi there' -o thinking 1 --usage Outputs: First I consider the prompt, then I decide what to say. { "prompt": "hi there", "system": "", "attachments": [], "stream": true, "previous": [] } Token usage: 2 input, 24 output Tags: llm
items.why_it_matters: A debug echo-model plugin for the LLM CLI that simulates token usage. It is a handy testing pattern but a minor release outside our core tools.
